idiom_name: RAII gateway class owning a CURL* handle (libcurl)
implementation_notes: The classic realization is an RAII class that owns the foreign handle and exposes domestic methods: the CURL* easy handle (or the vendor handle) lives in a constructor/destructor pair, or behind std::unique_ptr with a custom deleter, and the header never includes the vendor header. Typed method parameters replace the foreign string-concatenation signatures, and CURLcode is translated into the project's error type (exception or expected-like) inside the class. Keep it non-copyable and movable - and note that the class form is still justified even when the generated-client form exists, because it is where cross-cutting policy and the domestic type mapping are owned.
pitfalls: Rule of five: a wrapper that owns a CURL* handle and is copied double-frees it; delete the copy operations or write them deliberately.

A raw CURL* member in the header forces <curl/curl.h> into every translation unit that includes the gateway - use a pimpl or an out-of-line destructor with an incomplete type to keep the foreign vocabulary out.
Never let an exception escape through a C callback or a destructor: the C library reports failures as codes, so translate them explicitly at the boundary.

variants.name: protoc-generated gRPC stub class over grpc::Channel
variants.implementation_notes: When the foreign system publishes a protobuf/IDL contract, the generated C++ code already is the connection and most of the gateway: the protoc plugin emits a RouteGuide class whose NewStub(channel) returns a stub with one method per rpc, and grpc::ClientContext carries per-call deadlines, metadata and cancellation. The remaining domestic work is to map application types to the generated request/response messages and to translate grpc::Status into the project's error type; wrap the stub in a thin class so the generated headers do not spread through the code base. Choose this over a hand-written HTTP wrapper whenever the counterpart is gRPC - rewriting the transport by hand adds nothing.
pitfalls: grpc::Status is reported separately from the reply: a call that fails leaves a default-constructed response, so ignoring the status silently returns empty data.
The generated stub is designed to be shared across threads, but grpc::ClientContext is per call and must outlive it - sharing one context between concurrent calls is a race.
Returning generated protobuf types from the gateway's own interface re-introduces exactly the foreign coupling the gateway exists to remove.
